tip: 'La sal' is feminine – nouns ending in a consonant don't follow the -o/-a rule.
'Se me hace bola' – it 'turns into a ball' in my mouth, like food you can't swallow. A go-to idiom for tasks that feel impossibly heavy, like this 'informe'.
'Llevar' + time = to take (time). Like 'gustar', the time is the subject: 'twenty minutes takes me.' Also 'me llevó' (past).
'Están secas', not 'son secas': the dryness is a fixable current state – exactly what 'estar' is for. 'Son' would make 'dry' the hands' permanent trait.
Trading? That's 'por'. 'Lo cambiaron por otro modelo' – 'por' marks what you swap or pay in exchange, where English just says 'for.'
Sounds blunt? 'Quiero tres noches' is normal transactional Spanish – 'I want' isn't rude at a hotel desk. Save 'quisiera' for extra-polite requests.
Why 'termines,' not 'terminas'? 'Cuando' pointing at the future takes subjunctive – the finishing hasn't happened yet, so Spanish flags it as not-yet-real.
'Hacer' is used for weather: 'hace calor' (it's hot), 'hace frío' (it's cold).
'Sé' is knowing facts and info – like 'dónde está.' Knowing a person or place switches to 'conocer' – two knows in Spanish, each with its own job.
'Gustar' works backwards from English: the thing you like is the subject. 'Me gusta la ciudad' = the city pleases me. 'Me gustan los gatos' = cats please me (plural).
'Ilusión' here isn't 'illusion' – it's excited anticipation. 'Nos hace ilusión': the trip makes-us-thrill. Classic false friend: no delusions involved.
'Muy' (very) goes before adjectives/adverbs. For nouns, use 'mucho/a': 'mucha hambre,' not 'muy hambre.'
Trap: 'duermo solo seis horas' could also read 'I sleep ALONE six hours' – 'solo' means both only and alone. Context (or using 'solamente') breaks the tie.
'Hace frío' is literally 'it makes cold' – Spanish uses 'hacer' for weather. The same 'hace' means 'ago' with time ('hace dos años'), so context picks the meaning.
'Tener' + 'años' = to be X years old (Spanish uses 'have', not 'be').
English drops the article for beer-in-general; Spanish can't: 'la cerveza es muy barata' = beer as a whole is cheap. Generalizations normally take 'el/la/los/las'.
English says 'without sayING'; Spanish never puts -ing after a preposition: 'sin decir adiós' = without to-say goodbye. After 'sin', always the infinitive.
'Hay' = there is / there are. Unlike 'ser/estar', 'hay' is the same for singular and plural. Comes from 'haber'.
No apostrophe-s exists in Spanish: you say 'the house of my parents' – 'la casa de mis padres.' Owned thing first, then 'de' + owner, every time.
'Lo que' = what / that which: 'Lo que dices es verdad.' Used for abstract ideas or things not yet identified.
Why 'primer', not 'primero'? Before a masculine singular noun, 'primero' (and 'tercero') drop the -o: 'el primer día.' Everywhere else the -o stays.
'Date prisa' is literally 'give yourself haste' – in Spanish you hand hurry to yourself. Same logic as 'darse cuenta' (give yourself account = realize).
'Llevar' can mean 'to contain' for food: '¿lleva alguno?' = does it contain any? 'Ser alérgico a' = to be allergic to.
'Faltar' flips English: 'tiempo' is the subject – time is-missing on us. In Spanish you don't lack things; things go missing on you. Hence 'nos', not 'nosotros' as subject.
Fear isn't something you ARE in Spanish – things GIVE it to you: 'me da miedo' = it gives me fear. Same pattern: 'me da vergüenza' (embarrassment), 'me da pena'.
'Lo más importante': with no noun to point at, Spanish uses neuter 'lo' for 'the important thing'. 'El más importante' would mean a specific one.
'Política' does double duty: policy AND politics. A 'política de teletrabajo' is a company policy; 'la política' on the news is politics. Context decides which.
'Cuesta' here isn't about money – 'me cuesta levantarme' means getting up costs me effort. 'Costar' covers both prices and difficulty.
Taller than ME? Spanish says 'que yo' – comparisons take subject pronouns ('yo', 'tú', 'él'), never 'mí'/'ti'. 'Más alto que mí' is the classic English-speaker slip.
'Por LA nariz,' not 'mi nariz' – with body parts Spanish skips the possessive, since whose nose is obvious. Using 'mi' with your own body sounds oddly clinical.
